title: Test Levels and Test Types in Practice
concept:
Test levels and test types are independent dimensions: at any level, you can perform any type. In practice, certain combinations dominate.

**Component testing** is heavily functional + white-box. Developers exercise their unit's logic, covering statements and branches. Non-functional tests at this level focus on time- and memory-bounded units (e.g., a sort that must run in O(n log n) within 100 ms).

**Integration testing** is functional + black-box at the interface level (does the API contract hold?), plus non-functional (does the interface handle load? does it time out gracefully?). White-box techniques are used for protocol coverage.

**System testing** is dominated by functional + black-box (end-to-end scenarios from requirements) and non-functional + black-box (performance, security, usability of the whole system). Some white-box techniques (e.g., transaction flow coverage) appear too.

**Acceptance testing** is functional + black-box (business scenarios against user requirements) plus selected non-functional checks (does the system meet contractual response-time SLA? is it usable enough for the operator?).

The table of combinations is a useful tool when planning: for each level, decide which types and which techniques.
keyPoints: Levels (component, integration, system, acceptance) and types (functional, non-functional, black-box, white-box) are independent dimensions.
Component testing emphasises white-box functional; system and acceptance emphasise black-box functional plus non-functional.
Mapping test types to test levels in the test plan ensures balanced coverage of quality characteristics.

quiz.question: Which combination of test level and test type is MOST typical for verifying that a sorting function processes 10,000 items in under 200 ms?
quiz.explanation: A timing constraint on a single function is exercised at the component level (the function is the unit) and is non-functional (it's about performance, not correctness of the sort output). The other combinations test broader scopes than needed.
